summary: Limits the DNS KEY resource record to keys used by DNSSEC. The original KEY record could store both DNSSEC and arbitrary application keys, which was a mistake, so this redefines the protocol octet field and removes application keys from it. It was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS had one drawer for all kinds of keys. This note says that drawer is only for the DNS security system, and other keys go elsewhere. It was later replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

questions: why was dns key rr limited
what happened to dns email keys
subtitle: Limit the DNS KEY record to DNSSEC keys only, removing application keys.

tldr.problem: The DNS KEY resource record was designed to hold both DNSSEC keys and arbitrary application keys (email, IPSEC, TLS), but these two types are managed differently and have different security consequences. Mixing them creates unnecessary complexity and deployment problems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3445 redefines the Protocol Octet field of the KEY record to accept only value 3 (DNSSEC). All other values—Email (1), IPSEC (2), TLS (4)—are marked reserved. This removes application keys from the KEY record entirely and closes the registry to new assignments.
tldr.outcome: The KEY record is now used only for DNSSEC, simplifying the security model. RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 later consolidated the DNSSEC specification and replaced this record structure.

today: RFC 3445 restricts the DNS KEY record to DNSSEC keys only and closes the protocol octet registry. It updates RFC 2535 and was later consolidated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, which define the modern DNSSEC specification.

sections.title: The Mixing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2535 introduced the KEY resource record to store public keys in DNS, using sub-types to distinguish DNSSEC keys from application keys like Email, IPSEC and TLS keys. Over time, this mixing created problems. DNSSEC keys are managed by DNS administrators and are essential to the DNS infrastructure, but application keys are just data—they are managed by application administrators and have no special meaning to DNS.

The two types differ in virtually every respect: purpose, management, authentication rules, how name servers use them and how resolvers process them. Storing both in the same record adds unnecessary complexity. Limited deployment has shown application keys in KEY records are problematic.
sections.plainLanguage: It seemed like a good idea to use one type of record for all kinds of keys. In practice, DNS security keys and app keys are so different that they should not share a drawer. One compromise key could break the entire DNS.

sections.title: Differences Between Key Types
sections.content:
DNSSEC keys sign resource record sets and are used by name servers and resolvers to verify DNS data. A zone key signs the zone's entire record set. Application keys like Email, IPSEC or TLS keys are application-specific data with no special meaning to DNS.

DNSSEC keys are managed by DNS administrators, authenticated as part of a chain of trust with parent zones, included in DNS responses when useful and affect all data in a zone if compromised. Application keys are managed by their respective applications, are never part of a DNS chain of trust, are typically not useful to include in responses unless explicitly requested, and affect only that application if compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS keys protect the entire DNS. App keys protect just one app. If a DNS key is stolen, attackers can forge any DNS answer. If an app key is stolen, only that app is at risk. They are not the same kind of thing.

sections.title: The Revised KEY Record
sections.content:
The KEY resource record format itself is not changed. Instead, the Protocol Octet field—which distinguishes between sub-types—is restricted to value 3 only. DNSSEC is the only allowed value. All other protocol values (Email, IPSEC, TLS, and any future assignment) are marked RESERVED.

In the flags field, most bits are eliminated. Only bit 7 (the zone key bit) remains meaningful. All other flag bits MUST be set to zero and ignored by receivers. This simplification removes the A/C bits, the extended flags bit, the host/user bit and the signatory field.
sections.plainLanguage: The KEY record now has just one role: storing DNSSEC keys. All the extra knobs that were designed for other uses are turned off and ignored.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
DNSSEC zone keys are fully backward compatible. A properly formatted RFC 2535 zone KEY has all flag bits except bit 7 set to zero and protocol octet value 3. This remains true under the restriction.

DNSSEC non-zone keys used for SIG(0) and TKEY are backward compatible but lose the distinction between host and user keys. No backward compatibility is provided for Email, IPSEC or TLS keys—they are now deprecated. Name servers and resolvers that process KEY RRs with DNSSEC keys will continue to work correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Real DNS security keys still work exactly as before. Old email and IPSEC keys in DNS will be ignored. This is by design—they should not have been there in the first place.

sections.title: Status and Future Direction
sections.content: RFC 3445 removes application keys from the KEY record and closes the IANA registry to new protocol octet assignments. It updates RFC 2535 and is part of the transition toward cleaner DNSSEC specifications. The security model is simplified: KEY records contain only DNSSEC keys, managed by DNS administrators for DNS purposes. Later, RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 consolidated and replaced this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a cleanup step that made DNS security cleaner and simpler. Other RFCs came along later to finish the job and define how DNSSEC really works today.
